xrdbi: 'DBI' Backend for 'xarray' via a Live 'reticulate' Session

Source: R/xrdbi-package.R
xrdbi-package.Rd

Treats a live Python session holding an 'xarray' https://xarray.dev object as a database connection. Tables are variables, fields are dimensions and coordinates, and queries are Python expressions (or compiled from a small structured spec or from 'dplyr' verbs) evaluated lazily against the dataset. Fetching renders the tidy long form, one row per cell, built in R from the values; results can also render as an in-memory raster.

Articles

The package website has a Get started guide and articles with live examples: querying with dplyr, parameters, the shape and types of results, data sources, rasters, chunk maps, curvilinear grids and vector cubes, Python environments, and design notes.

How xarray maps to DBI

A connection holds one xarray Dataset, open in the Python session.

  • Tables are its variables, data variables and coordinates alike: DBI::dbListTables() lists them all, while dbGetInfo()$tables lists only the data variables.

  • The fields of a table are its dimensions, then its non-dimension coordinates, then the variable itself: the columns its rows will have (DBI::dbListFields()).

  • A statement is a Python expression over ds (the Dataset) and xr (the module), such as "ds.sst.isel(time=0)". It runs when sent; a selection reads nothing there, a computation runs in full (see XarrayResult).

  • Fetching renders the result in long form, as xarray's to_dataframe().reset_index() would: one row per cell, a column per coordinate. Missing floats stay NaN, times become POSIXct in UTC (as xarray stores them), and the geometry of a vector data cube becomes a wk::wkb() vector with its CRS when wk is installed (WKT strings otherwise).

Functions by task

  • Connect: xarray() is the driver; dbConnect() opens a path or URL, runs a builder function, or adopts a Python object; dbDisconnect() closes it.

  • Look around: print the connection, or use dbListTables(), dbListFields() and dbGetInfo() (XarrayConnection).

  • Query in Python: dbGetQuery(con, statement), or dbSendQuery() then dbFetch() in pages; pass values from R with params and rebind with dbBind() (XarrayResult). xr_query() writes a statement from a structured selection.

  • Query with dplyr: tbl() gives a lazy table for filter(), select(), head() and collect(), compiled to a statement that dplyr::show_query() prints.

  • Read a whole variable: dbReadTable().

  • Render other ways: xr_raster() gives a 2-D or 3-D slab in gdalraster's in-memory raster form; xr_chunks() maps the storage chunks a selection touches.

  • Use Python directly: xr_dataset() and xr_module() return the Dataset and the xarray module, unconverted.

Guards and options

Reads that materialize data are guarded: above a size they error, naming the size, unless the call is given force = TRUE. Each guarded function also takes the threshold as an argument; the options set the defaults.

  • xrdbi.max_cells (default 1e7): the most cells a read renders: the first dbFetch() of a result (so dbGetQuery()), dbReadTable(), collect() of a tbl_xarray, and xr_raster(). It sizes the result of a statement, not its computation: .mean('time') runs at dbSendQuery(), before the guard sees the result.

  • xrdbi.max_chunks (default 1e6): the most rows xr_chunks() returns.

  • xrdbi.print_n (default 6): the rows a printed tbl_xarray previews, reading at most one chunk.

  • xrdbi.print_preview (default TRUE): FALSE prints a tbl_xarray's compiled statement without the preview's data read (compiling still reads coordinates).

R packages used when installed

  • wk: geometry. Vector cube geometry arrives as wk::wkb() (WKT strings without it), geometry params are sent through it, and xr_chunks() returns each chunk's rectangle as a wk::rct().

  • sf: not needed, but sf::st_as_sfc() converts any of those.

  • gdalraster: not needed by xr_raster(), but its output is in the form gdalraster's read_ds() returns, so plot_raster() takes it.

Python requirements

Loading xrdbi declares its core Python requirements with reticulate::py_require(): 'xarray' (which brings 'pandas' and 'numpy') and 'netCDF4', the netCDF engine for local netCDF-3 and netCDF-4 files. When no Python is configured, reticulate provisions them in a managed environment on first use. Declare the IO engines your data needs the same way, before connecting (or after: reticulate then switches to an environment that adds them):

  • zarr stores: reticulate::py_require("zarr"), with "gcsfs" or "s3fs" for cloud buckets

  • netCDF/HDF5 over HTTPS via h5netcdf: reticulate::py_require(c("h5netcdf", "h5py", "fsspec", "aiohttp"))

  • many files as one dataset (open_mfdataset): reticulate::py_require("dask")

  • vector data cubes: reticulate::py_require(c("xvec", "geopandas"))

The 'gdalxarray' engine needs the GDAL Python bindings, which pip cannot install: use a conda environment (conda-forge gdal) or an image with GDAL, such as ghcr.io/hypertidy/gdal-r-python. With a Python you configure yourself (RETICULATE_PYTHON, a conda environment), install the packages there; reticulate does not provision into it.

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
## needs a Python environment with xarray (see Python requirements)
library(DBI)
f <- system.file("extdata/autotest/trmm.nc", package = "xrdbi")
con <- dbConnect(xarray(), f)
con
dbGetQuery(con, "ds.pcp.isel(time=0, latitude=0, longitude=slice(0, 3))")

library(dplyr)
tbl(con, "pcp") |> filter(latitude > -14, latitude < -13) |> collect()
dbDisconnect(con)
} # }
